\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling---self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}, extended reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}---yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks where outputs admit equivalence classes or execution-based verification.
For NER, where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, the boundary conditions for effective scaling are unknown; prior work reports task-level correlations \cite{yao2026consistency} and qualitative diversity collapse \cite{yun2025price} but no instance-level diagnostic framework.

Using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned; tentative cross-scale observations to 72B) and RE as case studies, we identify a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}: quality estimation signals predict output quality ($\rho$ up to $0.45$, AUROC $0.82$; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), yet selection fails---MV gains ${<}1$\,pp even at $N{=}64$ (Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling}; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
This gap decomposes into a definitional layer---four instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates---and an empirical one: LP, the only per-sample signal, also fails through within-instance compression (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
A hidden-state probe confirms models encode entity quality internally (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}), exposing an \textit{introspection boundary} \cite{huang2024large}.
A \textit{diagnostic framework} localizes the failure to two co-occurring conditions---degeneracy ($12$--$68$\%) and signal alignment collapse ($\alpha{\to}0$; $\alpha$ here denotes LP-F1 alignment)---which co-occur with selection failure (Table~\ref{tab:method_summary}).
The framework decomposes observed failures post-hoc rather than predicting which instances will fail a priori; our analysis is observational and all reported associations are correlational, not causal.
The optimal strategy is dataset-dependent (LP $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD; MV $+0.61$\,pp on CoNLL), and RE reveals a distinct bottleneck ($40$\% zero-F1; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
Exploratory entity-level construction yields conditional improvement ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, 3-epoch; global Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$, suggestive; per-family $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$, post-hoc family partition; diminishes at convergence) where the framework identifies favorable conditions---low degeneracy and LP-F1 alignment---but inverse scaling in most $N$-transitions confirms that scaling is harmful in the majority of configurations.

These findings rest on four NER benchmarks, two model families with 4B--72B ablations, $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 64\}$, and exploratory extensions to RE\footnote{RE F1 is confounded by entity span errors: the majority of zero-F1 RE instances reflect upstream NER mismatches rather than relation classification failure (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).} and SQL parsing ($87.2$\% degeneracy).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap (diagnostic sequence, not causal chain; Qwen3-8B fine-tuned, Few-NERD, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: LP-weighted entity construction ($\theta{=}2/N$) yields conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our investigation proceeds in three stages:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Discover} [\S\ref{sec:qe_results}].
QE signals achieve AUROC up to $0.82$; while \citet{yao2026consistency} report task-level correlation ($\rho$ up to 0.47), our instance-level decomposition reveals why correlation does not yield selection gains.
\item \textbf{Diagnose} [\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}].
A diagnostic cascade---degeneracy, LP compression, signal alignment---quantifies failure mechanisms at entity level; \citet{yun2025price} describe diversity collapse qualitatively, we provide quantitative decomposition ($D$, $\alpha$, LP range). A necessary condition bound (\S\ref{sec:theory}) confirms $\alpha$ as the binding constraint (3--12\% recovery ratio). Hidden-state probes reveal an introspection boundary (AUROC $0.63$--$0.88$ vs.\ ESJ $\approx 0.50$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}).
\item \textbf{Construct (exploratory)} [\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}].
Entity-level construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD where the cascade identifies favorable conditions. Unlike \citet{xie2023zeroshot}'s zero-shot entity voting, we aggregate stochastic samples from fine-tuned models.
\end{enumerate}

The paper is organized as follows: \S\ref{sec:related} contextualizes our contributions relative to prior art; \S\ref{sec:method} defines the diagnostic framework and confidence signals; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap} establishes the correlation-selection gap; \S\ref{sec:adaptive} evaluates adaptive methods; \S\ref{sec:theory_scaling} provides scaling analysis and degeneracy decomposition; \S\ref{sec:experiments} presents the main experimental results.

\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present exploratory attempts informed by diagnostic findings to extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.
Table~\ref{tab:method_summary} summarizes all 9 method categories evaluated; only cross-model ensembles yield a positive result, though on a single dataset.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Summary of 9 method categories tested (including MV baseline, LP selection, and cross-model ensemble beyond self-verification methods in Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic} and adaptive methods in this section). $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy; dataset in parentheses. Full coverage in Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}.}
\label{tab:method_summary}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrl@{}}
\toprule
Category & Method & $\Delta$F1 / metric & § \\
\midrule
Freq.\ voting & MV & baseline & \ref{sec:prescriptive} \\
LP selection & Best-of-$N$ (LP) & $+1.39$\,pp (FN)$^\dagger$ & \ref{sec:selection_gap} \\
Self-verif.\ (prompt) & ESJ & AUROC $0.51$ & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Multi-round refine. & MRSC & $-3.1$\,pp (FN) & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Latent aggregation & LSC & $-3.5$\,pp (FN) & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Adaptive gating & DALS & $+0.71$\,pp (SciERC)$^\ddagger$ & App.~\ref{app:dals} \\
Supervised verifier & LGB & $+0.30$\,pp (OOF) & \ref{sec:verifier} \\
Sup.\ combination & LR/MLP/RF & $-0.4$ to $-3.1$\,pp & App.~\ref{app:supervised_combination} \\
Cross-model & Qwen$+$LLaMA & $\mathbf{+0.42}$\,pp (FN) & \ref{sec:cross_model} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Few-NERD only; SciERC $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$). $^\ddagger$Seed-sensitive ($\sigma{=}0.48$\,pp).}
\end{table}

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models can partially bypass within-model degeneracy.
Combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (Few-NERD) yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA ($p{<}0.001$, CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total).
This observation is preliminary (single dataset, $n{=}4{+}4$ samples); cross-dataset validation is needed before drawing general conclusions.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ out-of-fold but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp overall: frequency-based construction already captures most verifier signal.
Cross-dataset transfer is negative ($-0.76$ to $-1.02$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), as feature importance shifts across entity-type complexity---even near-perfect entity classification cannot close the gap.

We have performed a **systematic claim downgrade** throughout the paper: causal→correlational, prescriptive→exploratory, four-stage→three-stage contributions, and power-aware negative claims. 2. **§4** reports all selection gains with CI language: "LP achieves +0.2 pp (p=0.29), below MDE (≈1.5 pp at n=529, 2–3 seeds)" (single_signal.tex, line 39).

\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}

\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}

Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), consistent with utility degradation on structured outputs \cite{eikema2025structured}.
We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).

\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}

Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).

\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).

\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}

\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).

\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.

\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.

MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.
